title: Alternating Current, Impedance and Resonance
subcategory: Alternating Current — AC Circuits, Impedance, Resonance, Transformer

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 12 — Alternating Current

summary: In an AC circuit, resistors, inductors and capacitors respond differently to a changing current (inductors and capacitors introduce a phase difference between current and voltage), combining into a total 'impedance'; a series LCR circuit driven at its natural resonant frequency allows maximum current to flow.
explanation: In a purely resistive AC circuit, current and voltage stay exactly in phase. In a purely inductive circuit, current LAGS voltage by 90° (inductors oppose CHANGE in current — di/dt — so their opposition, called inductive reactance XL = ωL, increases with frequency); in a purely capacitive circuit, current LEADS voltage by 90° (capacitive reactance Xc = 1/ωC decreases with frequency, since a capacitor charges/discharges more easily at low frequency). In a series LCR circuit, impedance Z = √(R² + (XL−Xc)²) combines all three effects, and current I = V/Z is generally out of phase with voltage by an angle φ where tanφ = (XL−Xc)/R. Average power dissipated is P = VrmsIrms cosφ, where cosφ is the 'power factor' — power is dissipated only in the resistive part; ideal inductors and capacitors, over a full cycle, dissipate NO net energy (they store and return it). Resonance occurs when XL = Xc (i.e., ω = ω₀ = 1/√(LC)), at which impedance is purely resistive and minimum (Z = R), so current is maximum — the basis of tuning a radio receiver to a specific station's frequency. A transformer uses electromagnetic induction (mutual inductance between primary and secondary coils sharing an iron core) to step voltage up or down: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np = Ip/Is (ideal, lossless transformer conserves power VpIp = VsIs), used to minimise transmission losses by transmitting electrical power at very high voltage (hence low current, low I²R loss) over long distances.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming impedance simply adds like resistances in series (Z = R + XL + Xc) — because of the 90° phase differences, XL and Xc must be combined by SUBTRACTING them (since they're exactly out of phase with each other) before combining with R using the Pythagorean-like formula.

Believing an ideal inductor or capacitor dissipates power in an AC circuit — over a complete cycle they store and fully return energy, dissipating zero net average power; only resistance dissipates power.
Thinking a step-up transformer increases power — an ideal transformer conserves power exactly; a step-up in voltage always comes with a proportional step-DOWN in current.
examples: A radio tuning circuit is adjusted (usually by varying capacitance) until the circuit resonates at the desired station's broadcast frequency, maximising signal current.
Power is transmitted over long distances at very high voltage (and correspondingly low current) specifically to reduce I²R heating losses in the transmission wires.
genZNote: Inductor and capacitor: perpetually 90° out of sync, but resonance is when they finally cancel each other out.
